newsitem.title: SPAIN: Spain wage inflation not ready for EMU - analysts.
newsitem.headline: Spain wage inflation not ready for EMU - analysts.

text.p: Spanish wages are rising at more than double the consumer price index rate, fanning medium-term inflation fears and spotlighting an area where Spain is ill-prepared for Europe's single currency.
On Monday, Spain reported that first-quarter wages rose 4.2 percent a month on average, while the monthly inflation rate was 2.2 percent in March, 1.7 percent in April and 1.5 in May.
Although economists foresee a slowdown in wage gains, they say the moderation must be sizeable if Spain is to be competitive within European economic and monetary union (EMU).

"If Spain wants to stay in a single currency with Germany they have to reduce this rate toward two percent," said Giorgio Radaelli, economist at Lehman Brothers in London. "Otherwise they will have growing problems in selling goods outside Spain."
He said a new labour market reform, which took effect in mid-May, will tend to limit trade union power and thus wage inflation.

Also sustained economic growth -- with gross domestic product seen climbing at least three percent year-on-year in 1997 -- will boost productivity and contain the inflationary effect of wage increases.
But until these factors kick in, the Spanish central bank is likely to share economists' concerns.
In May, speaking to a parliamentary commission, Bank of Spain governor Luis Angel Rojo said: "wages have not adapted at a quick enough rate to the steadier inflation outlook.
"This adjustment of wages to the new low inflation outlook ..is an imperative in order to participate in EMU."
Also on Monday, the Bank of Spain left its key money rate unchanged at 5.25 percent although the new fall in the inflation rate in May gave it scope to ease monetary policy further.

Many analysts said the Spanish central bank was simply awaiting the end of the Amsterdam European Union summit and final approval of the budget stability pact before moving ahead and sanctioning its fifth official rate cut this year.
"It's likely they will cut rates in eight days, after the EU summit. After that they will take a long rest," said Henrik Lumholdt, chief economist at Bank of America in Madrid.
"The 1997 inflation trend is pretty clear..people need not fear it reigniting," he said. "If there is a pick-up it will be due to less favourable comparisons (versus the year earlier)."
"But in 1998, inflation could raise worries, especially if wage (increases) continue, given the risk of possible increases in special taxes on cigarettes and alcohol," Lumholdt added.
Spanish media rumours have suggested special taxes may be hiked as a way of raising funds to reform the health system on a regional basis.
"At least longer term, this (high rate of wage inflation) should tend to push inflation higher," said Lehman's Radaelli.
But other analysts were less worried.
"Today's data is pretty high... The purchasing power of wages is recovering from a period when it was falling," said Francesco Giordano at Credit Suisse First Boston in London.
"If wages cool down slowly that is good because (it means) they will take a while to pick up when inflation does," he added.
